title: Tokens all the way down
summary: Cooperative cancellation, where tokens come from in ASP.NET Core, checking in loops, linked tokens, and the exceptions that carry it.

steps.title: Cancellation is a request, not a kill
body: .NET never stops your code from the outside. A `CancellationTokenSource` (CTS) owns the *switch*; the `CancellationToken` it hands
out can only *see* the switch. Code that is asked to stop must look and stop itself:
- async APIs that take a token (`HttpClient`, EF Core, `Task.Delay`, `Channel` reads, `SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync`) stop waiting and throw
`OperationCanceledException` when it is cancelled;
- CPU loops call `ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested()` every so often;
- `ct.Register(() => ...)` runs a callback on cancellation (to abort something that has no token).
In ASP.NET Core, a `CancellationToken` parameter on an endpoint is bound to `HttpContext.RequestAborted`: it fires when the client
disconnects. If you do not pass it down, the database query keeps running for a user who left.
```csharp fragment
app.MapGet("/orders/{id}", async (int id, OrdersDb db, CancellationToken ct) =>
await db.Orders.FindAsync([id], ct) is { } o ? Results.Ok(o) : Results.NotFound());
`TaskCanceledException` derives from `OperationCanceledException`: catch the base type.

steps.prompt: Match each piece to its job.
pairs: lets code observe the switch, cannot flip it
a check point inside a CPU-bound loop
fires when the HTTP client disconnects

steps.title: Linked tokens: more than one reason to stop
body: A request handler usually has two reasons to stop: **the client went away** and **our own time budget ran out**. Combine them:
```csharp fragment
using var budget = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(requestAborted);
budget.CancelAfter(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2));
try
return await inventory.GetAsync(sku, budget.Token);
catch (OperationCanceledException) when (!requestAborted.IsCancellationRequested)
return Fallback(sku);          // our timeout fired: degrade gracefully
}                                   // the client left: let the exception go, nobody is listening
- The linked source cancels when **any** parent cancels, or when its own timer fires.
- **Dispose** linked and timed sources (`using`): they register callbacks on their parents and hold a timer.
- The `when` filter tells *which* reason fired. Never treat every `OperationCanceledException` as a timeout.

steps.explain: Cancellation flows from parent to child, never back up. Cancelling the linked source does not cancel the token it was made from.

steps.prompt: A call was cancelled. In the `catch (OperationCanceledException)`, which ones are *our timeout* and which mean *the caller gave up*?
items: The user closed the browser tab mid-request
steps.explain: Since .NET 5, `HttpClient` marks its own timeout with an inner `TimeoutException`, so you can tell it apart from your token. For your own budget, check which token is cancelled.

steps.prompt: Make the CPU-bound loop stop promptly when asked.
code: static long Checksum(byte[][] blocks, CancellationToken ct)
foreach (var b in block) sum += b;
steps.explain: Check once per block, not once per byte: the check is cheap, but not free, and a block is small enough to keep the response prompt.

steps.title: A batch that stops between items
prompt: Write **`static async Task<int> ProcessBatchAsync(IReadOnlyList<string> items, Func<string, CancellationToken, Task> handle, CancellationToken ct)`**.
- Handle the items **one at a time, in order**, passing `ct` to `handle`.
- Before starting each item, stop if `ct` is cancelled by throwing `OperationCanceledException` (the usual way: `ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested()`).
- Return how many items were handled when it finishes normally.
The tests cancel the token while the second item is being handled: the third must never start, and the method must throw.
starter: static async Task<int> ProcessBatchAsync(IReadOnlyList<string> items, Func<string, CancellationToken, Task> handle, CancellationToken ct)
solution: static async Task<int> ProcessBatchAsync(IReadOnlyList<string> items, Func<string, CancellationToken, Task> handle, CancellationToken ct)
template: async Task DojoHandle(string item, CancellationToken ct)
await Dojo.ThrowsAsync<OperationCanceledException>("Cancelling during item b stops the batch with OperationCanceledException",
Dojo.Eq("Items a and b ran; c never started", new List<string> { "a", "b" }, dojoSeen);
Dojo.Check("The token is passed on to every item", dojoTokens.All(t => t == dojoCts.Token), "Call handle(item, ct), not CancellationToken.None.");
Dojo.Eq("An uncancelled batch handles every item", 3, await ProcessBatchAsync(new[] { "x", "y", "z" }, (_, _) => Task.CompletedTask, CancellationToken.None));
hints: Two changes: pass `ct` to `handle`, and check the token at the top of the loop.
`ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();` as the first line in the loop body, then `await handle(item, ct);`.
